title: Day and Night 1
content:
Wen Ning clamped his mouth shut. Over the steady, rhythmic splash of oars cutting through water, Wei Wuxian’s eyes fluttered open against a skull-splitting headache.

He was leaning heavily against Lan Wangji. It took him a disoriented second to realize they were no longer anywhere near Lotus Pier. His gaze drifted down to Lan Wangji’s left sleeve—speckled with dark crimson droplets like winter plum blossoms scattered over fresh snow. The memory of the blowout in the ancestral hall came rushing back, and his face twisted in utter mortification.

He scrambled upright. Lan Wangji reached out to steady him, but Wei Wuxian’s ears were still buzzing with static, his chest tight and suffocating with the metallic tang of blood.

Terrified of coughing up another mouthful of gore onto the notoriously fastidious Hanguang-jun, he waved him off in a panic, whipped around, and leaned over the gunwale to ride out the nausea. Lan Wangji knew better than to push. Without a word, he rested a palm between Wei Wuxian's shoulder blades, funneling a steady, soothing stream of spiritual energy into his battered meridians.

Only when the coppery taste in his throat finally receded did Wei Wuxian look back, signaling Lan Wangji to stop. He sat in uneasy silence for a moment before testing the waters: "Hanguang-jun... how did we get out of there?"

At the stern, Wen Ning went rigid, freezing over his oars. True to his word, Lan Wangji didn't breathe a single syllable about the truth Wen Ning had laid bare. But he didn't spin a lie either, answering flatly: "We fought."

Wei Wuxian pressed a fist to his sternum, trying to knead away the persistent ache behind his ribs. After an endless pause, he blew out a heavy breath. "I knew Jiang Cheng wouldn't just let us walk away. That little bastard... he's really lost his damn mind."

Lan Wangji’s brow pinched into a severe furrow. "Do not speak of him."

Startled by the uncharacteristic bite in his voice, Wei Wuxian backed down immediately. "Right. Fine. Dropping it."

He hesitated, turning his words over before adding carefully, "Hey. Hanguang-jun... don't take anything he said to heart, alright?"

"Which part?" Lan Wangji asked.

Wei Wuxian’s eyelid gave an involuntary twitch. "All of it. He's been like this since we were kids—the second he loses his temper, his filter flies right out the window. Just spits the foulest garbage he can think of, manners and upbringing be damned. If it hurts your feelings, he'll say it. Decades, and the guy hasn't grown up a single bit. Seriously, don't let it get to you."

He studied Lan Wangji's face as he spoke, his stomach slowly sinking.

He had hoped—maybe even assumed—that Lan Wangji would just brush it off. But Lan Wangji looked genuinely stone-faced, refusing to offer even his usual noncommittal hum.

It seemed Jiang Cheng’s venom had cut far deeper than Wei Wuxian thought. Maybe he just despised Jiang Cheng as a person. Or maybe... Lan Wangji couldn't stomach being branded as "indecent," "shameless," or "disreputable trash." After all, the Gusu Lan Clan literally carved righteousness and elegance into their cliffside rules. Hanguang-jun’s pristine reputation had never been dragged through the mud with words like that in his entire life.

Over the past few weeks, Wei Wuxian had started to feel like Lan Wangji cared for him—that there was something distinct, something different between them. But he never dared guess just how deep that regard ran, or if that "difference" was really what he secretly hoped it was. Confidence had never been a problem for him; he’d spent a lifetime strutting around with an arrogant grin, and rumors painted the grand Yiling Laozu as an effortless heartbreaker with a trail of romances in his wake. Yet the reality was embarrassingly pathetic: he was completely out of his depth. He used to think Lan Wangji was the easiest man in the world to read, but right now, he couldn't parse him at all. He was terrified that he was getting ahead of himself—overthinking things, caught up in wishful delusions.

With Lan Wangji wrapped in suffocating silence, Wei Wuxian wanted to crack a joke and laugh it off as usual, but he choked, terrified of making things infinitely more awkward. In the end, he blurted out an aggressively clunky pivot: "So... where are we headed?"

It was an embarrassingly stiff transition, but Lan Wangji rolled with it anyway. "Where do you wish to go?"

Wei Wuxian scratched the back of his neck. "We still don't know if Ze-wu-jun is safe, or what the other clans are planning. We could head to Lanling first..." He paused, a thought striking him. "Wait. Not Lanling. Let's hit Yunping City."

"Yunping City?"

"Yeah. Yunping, down in Yunmeng. I told you about this, right? Back at Koi Tower, when I broke into the hidden chamber in the Fragrance Palace, I found my stolen manuscripts. Tucked right beside them was a property deed for a plot in Yunping. The Lanling Jin Clan swims in gold and land—Jin Guangyao wouldn't stash a random deed in his personal vault unless it was hiding something massive. We might dig up some answers there."

Lan Wangji gave a slow nod.

Just then, a tentative voice drifted from the back: "Master, is Yunping City in this direction?"

Wei Wuxian jumped out of his skin. "What the hell?!"

Both he and Lan Wangji had been sitting with their backs to the stern, completely oblivious. The sudden, disembodied question spooked Wei Wuxian so hard he nearly rolled right off the bench, whipping around in pure terror. "Where did you crawl out from?!"

Wen Ning blinked back, looking completely lost. "Me? I... I've been here the whole time."

"Then why didn't you say anything?!"

"You and Hanguang-jun were talking," Wen Ning mumbled. "I didn't want to interrupt..."

"You couldn't have cleared your throat or something?!"

Wen Ning lifted an oar, looking wounded. "Master, I've been rowing non-stop. The water has been splashing this entire time. Did you really not hear me?"

After a beat, Wei Wuxian waved a dismissive hand, thoroughly defeated. "Didn't notice. Whatever, put the oars down. The river runs fast out here at night; the current will carry us just fine."

Having grown up diving and swimming across Yunmeng’s waterways, he knew these currents like the back of his hand. Wen Ning nodded obediently, stowed the oars, and retreated into a stiff, polite ball at the stern, keeping a strict six feet of clearance between himself and the two of them.

They had reached Lotus Pier in the dead of night, and after all that chaos, dawn was finally cracking over the horizon. The sky was a pale, milky blue, and the dark silhouettes of misty hills along the banks were slowly coming into focus.

Wei Wuxian scanned the landscape, his stomach suddenly grumbling. "I'm starving."

Lan Wangji looked over. Wei Wuxian wasn't actually hungry—he’d inhaled three whole flatbreads by the docks barely an hour ago. But Lan Wangji had only managed a single pastry. Aside from that tiny bite, the man hadn't had a proper meal in nearly two days. Wei Wuxian couldn't shake the worry, and seeing how deserted the riverbanks were, it would probably be hours before they bumped into an actual town with a warm kitchen.

Lan Wangji considered it. "Pull ashore?"

"There's nobody out here," Wei Wuxian said, leaning over the side. "But I know a spot."

Wen Ning scrambled for the oars, steering them toward a narrow inlet Wei Wuxian pointed out. Before long, the skiff cut into a quiet tributary, gliding into an endless, sprawling lake of wild lotuses.

Enormous lotus leaves rose in staggered layers, arching overhead like emerald parasols. The slender wooden skiff parted the dense, tangled stems, gliding straight into the heart of the marsh. Seen from above, the boat carved a single, rippling path through the sea of green. Weaving through the canopy of leaves, Wei Wuxian pushed aside a dinner-plate-sized lotus pad, revealing fat, heavy seed pods hiding beneath the shade. The sheer rush of it was like unearthing a secret stash of treasure. Grinning from ear to ear, he reached out to snap one off—

"Wei Ying."

Wei Wuxian paused, hand mid-air. "Yeah?"

Lan Wangji’s tone was dead even. "Does this lake belong to someone?"

Wei Wuxian put on a face of absolute, unblemished innocence. "Nope. Totally wild."

Of course it wasn't. Ever since he was eleven, Wei Wuxian had terrorized every privately owned lotus pond and water-caltrop patch across Yunmeng. He’d officially hung up his thieving boots years ago, but desperate times called for desperate measures—the old master had to come out of retirement to feed the crew.

Lan Wangji remarked coolly, "I have heard that every lotus pond in this region has an owner."

Wei Wuxian forced an awkward, wheezing chuckle. "Hahaha, really? Man, what a shame. You sure know an awful lot of gossip—even I hadn't heard that one. Guess we’ll just head out, then."

Now that he’d been called out, he couldn't very well drag the impeccably righteous Hanguang-jun into petty larceny. The Second Young Master of Gusu Lan poaching roadside lotus seeds? It sounded downright scandalous.

Sheepish, he turned to reach for an oar.

Just as his hand moved, Lan Wangji raised his arm, reached up, and cleanly snapped a ripe lotus pod right off its stem.

He held it out, dropping the heavy pod into Wei Wuxian’s lap.

"Just this once."
